bib.title: Statistical Rethinking, 1st ed., Chapter 10: Counting and Classification

question: How do you regress count outcomes (binomial and Poisson) on predictors while keeping sample-size information, and how should the resulting log-odds and log-rate parameters be interpreted?
contributions: Binomial regression (logistic and aggregated) worked on the chimpanzee and UC Berkeley data
Poisson regression worked on Oceanic tool counts, with offsets for varying exposure
Short sketches of multinomial, geometric, negative-binomial and beta-binomial models

results.claim: Intercept-only logistic model: chimpanzees pull the left lever with probability about 0.58 overall (a=0.32 log-odds).
results.setup: Chimpanzees data, m10.1, map, Normal(0,10) prior, 7 actors
results.quote: the above summary implies a MAP probability of pulling the left lever of logistic(0.32)≈0.58, with a 89% interval of 0.54 to 0.61

results.claim: WAIC ranks the prosocial-only model m10.2 first (weight 0.70) over the interaction model m10.3 (0.28).
results.setup: Chimpanzees, 3 models m10.1-m10.3, map, WAIC with SE 9.30
results.table: Table at R code 10.5, row m10.2, column WAIC
results.note: m10.3 WAIC 682.4 dWAIC 1.8 weight 0.28; m10.1 WAIC 688.0 dWAIC 7.4 weight 0.02

results.claim: Interaction of condition with prosocial option is near zero: bpC=-0.10 (sd 0.26, 89% interval -0.53 to 0.32), so the partner's presence made little difference.
results.table: Table at R code 10.6, row bpC, column Mean

results.claim: A log-odds coefficient of 0.61 multiplies odds by 1.84 (an 84% increase) but with intercept 4 changes probability by under 1 percentage point (0.982 to 0.990): relative effects mislead.
results.setup: Worked example from bp=0.61, hypothetical alpha=4
results.quote: So that’s a difference, on the absolute scale, of less than 1%, despite being an 84% increase in proportional odds.

results.claim: MAP and MCMC agree for m10.3: MCMC gives bp=0.62, bpC=-0.11, a=0.05 with n_eff about 3000 and Rhat 1, so the quadratic approximation is fine.
results.table: Table at R code 10.12, row bp, column Mean

results.claim: With a separate intercept per actor (m10.4, MCMC), the intercept for always-left actor 2 is a[2]=10.91 with sd 5.42 and a strongly skewed posterior; the data cannot tell large values apart.
results.setup: Chimpanzees, m10.4, map2stan, 2 chains, iter=2500, warmup=500, Normal(0,10) priors
results.table: Table at R code 10.16, row a[2], column Mean
results.note: bp rises to 0.84 (sd 0.28), bpC=-0.13 (sd 0.30); other intercepts range -1.05 to 1.83

results.claim: Aggregating chimpanzee data to counts out of 18 trials gives the same posterior as the 0/1 model m10.3.
results.setup: m10.5, map, 28 aggregated rows (7 actors x 4 treatments)
results.quote: Take note of the 18 in the spot where a 1 used to be.
results.note: The 28 row count is derived, not printed; text says four rows per actor.

results.claim: UC Berkeley admissions: 12 rows represent 4526 applications to 6 departments.
results.quote: These 12 rows however represent 4526 applications, the sum of the applications column.

results.claim: Pooled gender model m10.6 beats the intercept-only model by 91.5 WAIC points.
results.table: Table at R code 10.24, row m10.7, column dWAIC

results.claim: Ignoring department, a male applicant has 1.84 times the odds of admission (bm=0.61), a median 14% higher probability of admission (95% interval 11% to almost 17%).
results.quote: This means that the median estimate of the male advantage is about 14%, with a 95% interval from 11% to almost 17%.

results.claim: Adding department intercepts reverses the sign: bm=-0.10 (sd 0.08), men have about 90% of women's odds within departments.
results.quote: So a male in this sample has about 90% the odds of admission as a female, comparing within departments.

results.claim: Never convert counts to proportions before analysis: it destroys sample size information.
results.quote: It is important to never convert counts to proportions before analysis, because doing so destroys information about sample size.

results.claim: Quadratic approximation is typically accurate for binomial regression only if no intercept sits far from zero and no predictor is strongly associated with the outcome.
results.quote: is typical for binomial regression, as long as none of the intercepts are very far from zero, such that they push against the ceiling or floor, and none of the predictors are strongly associated with the outcome.

limits: Year 2016 is inferred from the first edition; the chapter text prints no date.
Uses the old rethinking API (map, map2stan, ensemble, compare with WAIC); later editions replaced these with ulam/quap.
Negative-binomial and beta-binomial are named but deferred to the next chapter; no worked examples for multinomial beyond simulation.
Kline island data has 10 rows; the author says the Normal(0,1) priors are probably not conservative enough.
Model comparison is not a guarantee: 'They are not forms of divination.'
The author's own MAP caveat: 'in principle no GLM is safe for MAP estimation'.
practices: Model counts, not proportions, to keep sample size (p.291, p.328).
Convert log-odds back to probability with the inverse link before interpreting; report absolute as well as relative (odds ratio) effects (p.294-297).
Check posterior predictions against data; a bad fit may be a good answer to the wrong question, as in the pooled gender model (p.306-307).
Add a per-group intercept (index variable) to control group heterogeneity, as department in UCBadmit (p.307).
Check quadratic approximation against MCMC for every GLM (p.298, 308, 319).
Use weakly regularizing priors instead of glm's flat priors, which fail under near-perfect separation (p.310-311).
Do not judge a predictor by marginal intervals alone when parameters are correlated; use counterfactual predictions or WAIC (p.315-317).
Centre predictors to reduce posterior correlations and raise n_eff (p.320-321).
Use log(exposure) as an offset when observation windows differ (p.312-313, 321-322).
Interpret multinomial models only through implied probabilities; estimates depend on the chosen reference event (p.325).
Use log of population when theory says order of magnitude matters (p.314).
WAIC for aggregated binomials is computed on disaggregated 0/1 points so it matches the logistic form (p.309).

terms.definition: the common name when the data are organized into single-trial cases, such that the outcome variable can only take values 0 and 1
individual trials with the same covariate values aggregated together; the outcome can take the value zero or any positive integer up to n, the number of trials
just a proportional change induced by a change in the predictor (for logistic, the proportional change in odds, exp of the coefficient)
the change in the probability of the outcome; depends on all of the parameters
special shape of the binomial when n is very large and p very small; expected value np approximately equals variance np(1-p); one parameter lambda, the expected value
tau, the unit of time or distance; adding log(tau) to the linear model without a parameter is the offset
a positive association in the entire population need not hold within each department; not a violation of logic, just of intuition
multinomial model with each event isolated on a single row; the machine-learning name is maximum entropy classifier
Pr(y|p) = p(1-p)^(y-1); y is the number of time steps until the terminating event
variation in the counts exceeds what we would expect from a pure binomial or Poisson process
